question: To run three coding agents in parallel on one machine, you weigh (a) three separate clones of the repo against (b) three linked worktrees of one repo. Hard requirement: an agent's commit must be reviewable from your main checkout the moment it is made. What is the architectural argument for worktrees?
choices: Separate clones would share .git/HEAD, so a checkout in one agent's clone would silently move the other agents onto its branch
Worktrees give each agent a private ref namespace, so their feature branches cannot collide with yours during review
Worktrees are registered with the remote as a unit, so CI sees all three agents' branches from a single push

Linked worktrees share one object store and ref namespace behind separate working trees, HEADs, and indexes — a commit made at any desk is instantly visible from every other with no push, fetch, or remote round-trip; clones would need a fetch cycle before every review
explanation: A linked worktree is a second desk in front of the same filing cabinet: files, HEAD, and index are per-worktree (agents cannot race each other's checkouts), while objects and refs are shared (a commit made in any worktree is immediately visible from the main one — git log --all and git diff main..feature/x work with zero synchronization). Clones isolate just as well but sever the shared store: every review would need a push from the agent's clone and a fetch into yours. The distractors invert the model — clones share nothing (each has its own HEAD, which is exactly the single-worktree race worktrees were built to fix), worktree refs are shared rather than private, and worktrees are local-only metadata that never reach the remote or CI.

question: Agent 1 is working in slot ../proj-agent1 with feature/task-1 checked out. To review its work you run git worktree add ../review feature/task-1 — and git refuses: the branch is already checked out elsewhere. What failure is this rule preventing, and what should you do instead?
choices: Two checkouts of one branch would fork the shared object store, duplicating every blob the branch touches until the stores are reconciled
The rule protects the remote: pushes from two worktrees on the same branch would create divergent refs on origin

Worktrees share a single ref namespace but each has its own HEAD, index, and files. With one branch checked out at two desks, a commit made at either silently moves the branch tip under the other, leaving its working tree and index based on a commit that is no longer the branch head — the same class of silent desync worktrees exist to fix. Review needs no checkout anyway: refs and objects are shared, so git log and git diff main..feature/task-1 work from the main desk; use --detach for a read-only checkout of the files
Each branch's reflog accepts writes from only one worktree, so a second checkout would corrupt the shared reflog
explanation: The worktree model splits .git into shared parts (objects, refs, config) and per-worktree parts (HEAD, index, working files). That split is exactly why a branch may live in only one worktree: the branch pointer is shared while the checked-out files are not, so two desks on one branch would race each other's commits — the mirror image of the shared-.git/HEAD race that motivated worktrees in the first place, which is why it's a safety check (bypassable with --force only knowingly). The refusal also points at the better workflow: because commits and refs are visible from every worktree instantly, reviewing an agent's branch requires no checkout at all — log, diff, and even merging from the main desk all work without touching the agent's slot; --detach covers the rare case where you need the files themselves. The distractors contradict the architecture: the object store is content-addressed, append-only, and shared — nothing forks; worktrees are local-only metadata that never reach origin or CI; and reflogs are per-ref bookkeeping, not a locking mechanism.

question: Reorganizing your disk, you mv ../proj-agent1 — a linked worktree where an agent has uncommitted work — to ../agents/slot1. Git commands inside the moved directory still seem to work, but git worktree list at the main desk shows the old path, annotated prunable. A teammate suggests running git worktree prune to clean things up. What does the design of worktree metadata say about that advice?
choices: Prune is precisely the wrong command: worktree linkage is a two-way pointer pair — the worktree's .git file points at the main repo's .git/worktrees/<name>/, and that metadata directory's gitdir file points back at the working directory. The mv broke only the back-pointer, which is why commands inside the moved tree still work (its own pointer is intact) while the main repo sees a worktree whose recorded path no longer exists — the meaning of 'prunable'. But prune's contract is cleanup after deletion: it removes metadata directories whose working trees are gone. Run it here and it deletes the metadata a live worktree still points at, orphaning a tree that holds uncommitted work. The fix is git worktree repair, which rewrites the stale back-pointer; the prevention is git worktree move, which relocates the directory and updates metadata as one operation. Prune is for manual deletes; repair is for manual moves

The advice is safe: all commits live in the shared object store, so prune loses nothing — afterwards, git worktree add ../agents/slot1 re-registers the moved directory in place and the agent continues where it left off

There is nothing to fix: the moved worktree's own .git pointer is intact, which is why git works inside it — the prunable annotation is cosmetic bookkeeping that clears the next time the worktree runs any command that touches the main repository
Worktrees cannot be relocated — the paths are fixed at add time — so the procedure is: commit or stash the agent's work, remove the old worktree, and create a fresh one at the new path
explanation: The scenario probes whether you know what 'prunable' measures and which invariant a manual mv breaks. A linked worktree is held together by two pointers: forward (worktree's .git file → metadata dir) and backward (metadata's gitdir file → worktree path). Moving the directory by hand updates neither, but only the backward pointer is now wrong — so the asymmetry in symptoms is exact: inside the tree everything resolves, while the main repo, following its stale back-pointer to a path that no longer exists, concludes the worktree was deleted and marks it prunable. That annotation is a deletion hypothesis, and it happens to be false. Prune acts on the hypothesis: it exists so that after a genuine rm -rf you can clear the orphaned metadata. Running it after a move destroys the metadata directory that the moved worktree's forward pointer targets — converting a half-broken linkage into a fully orphaned working tree, with the agent's uncommitted work stranded in a directory Git no longer recognizes. Repair is the inverse tool: it re-derives the back-pointers from the worktrees' own forward pointers. The distractors fail on the same asymmetry: prune-then-re-add discards the uncommitted index and working state that only that directory holds (add wants a clean slate, and the commits being safe in the object store doesn't save the dirty files); 'cosmetic' underestimates prunable — automated expiry (gc.worktreePruneExpire) or any teammate's routine prune acts on it destructively; and 'worktrees can't move' ignores both git worktree move and repair, whose entire purpose is this situation.
